title: Dynamic mini-window admission & KV-pressure throttling for sustained peak QPS
creator: Maya Chen
description:
Goal: Reduce 95th/99th token latency and tail request rejection during sustained high QPS by introducing a dynamic
'mini-window' admission controller and a KV-pressure-aware throttling policy. This ticket covers design, simulation, prototype, and canary rollout for the new admission/eviction controls that operate alongside existing continuous batching.

Background:
- Continuous batching has reduced average cost but under high sustained QPS we observe GPU memory pressure and KV cache churn that leads to long tails and occasional dropped requests when headroom is exhausted.
- Current heuristics are static microbatch thresholds and a single global KV eviction watermark. These don't adapt to mixed request mixes (short-chat vs long-generation) or transient spikes with many cold prefixes.

Proposal summary:
1) Mini-window admission: replace fixed-size microbatch gate with a time-windowed admission that adapts window length and max-window-item based on running estimates of GPU KV residency and per-request expected token work. The controller uses a short-term EWMA of slot utilization and a per-model rolling distribution of generation lengths.
2) KV-pressure triage: annotate requests with a KV-residency score (hot|warm|cold) computed from prefix-hash hits and last-access recency. Incoming requests are ranked; admission favors hot/warm to preserve cache hit-rate during pressure. Cold requests get optional lightweight fallbacks or are queued behind soft backpressure.
3) Two-tier backpressure: (soft) accept-but-delay with progressive batching when headroom is low; (hard) reject-with-retry-after when thresholds hit sustained critical pressure. Soft backpressure uses incremental batching timeouts and KV prefetch hints.
4) Adaptive eviction policy: instead of a global LRU-only policy, we add a residency+importance score where tokens that accelerate future prefixes (prompt templates, system prefixes) get extended residency. Eviction aggressiveness is a function of observed tail latency and QPS.

Success metrics (canary baseline vs new controller):
- 99th-token latency reduced by >= 20% under sustained QPS 1.5x peak baseline
- Tail rejection rate (429/503) lowered to < 0.1% over 1h rolling window
- KV hit-rate degradation < 3% on mixed workloads
- No more than 5% increase in median cost-per-token (acceptable trade for tail improvement)

Rollout plan:
- Phase A: Simulation + offline trace-replay (2 weeks). Run against 7 days of production traces with injected spikes.
- Phase B: Prototype behind feature flag on a small pool (5% capacity) with detailed telemetry. Canary for 48h.
- Phase C: Gradual ramp with automated rollback if 99th latency or rejection exceed thresholds.

Instrumentation & observability needs:
- New metrics: kv_residency_ratio, mini_window_size, admission_queue_depth, soft_backpressure_rate, hard_reject_rate, per-prefix_eviction_score
- Add tracing tags for admission_decision and kv_score to link to Console dashboards and error-analysis pipelines

Testing plan:
- Unit tests for admission logic (time-window variations, scoring)
- Integration tests with local GPU runtime emulator and KV-mock to validate eviction behavior under synthetic churn
- Load test with k6 replaying production traces, validate metrics against success criteria

Risks & mitigations:
- Risk: Overly aggressive favoring of hot prefixes could starve new users. Mitigation: fairness token that guarantees a minimum admission fraction for cold requests over time windows.
- Risk: Complexity increase leads to new latency sources. Mitigation: keep decision path in C++ fast path, fall back to existing controller if evaluation cost exceeds budget.
- Risk: Incorrect KV scoring may misclassify. Mitigation: conservative initial thresholds, deploy with shadow mode for two days to compare decisions vs baseline.

Dependencies: ENG-41234, ENG-56024, runtime PRs that expose per-request prefix fingerprints and KV access telemetry. See dependencies list below.
